seo.title: Karmic tail 15 11 14 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 15 11 14 compatibility: the Devil at the entry, Strength in the middle, Temperance as the main task — and the myth of Heracles sold to Queen Omphale.

title: Karmic tail 15-11-14 in compatibility: from “you're mine” to “us”
short: You will not find 15-11-14 in any personal matrix: for the Devil to lead into Temperance, the centre of the chart would have to hold the Magician, and in a single person's chart it never does. Only two people can make this tail, and in compatibility it tells the story of the bond itself — how it travels from “you're mine” to “us”. The Devil at the entry is the wish to belong to each other, so strong that it borders on the wish to own. Strength in the middle is a trial of strength: who has tamed whom. Temperance as the main task is an exchange in which the same person does not always give way and each stays themselves.

sections.h2: Why only a couple can have this tail
paragraphs: In a personal matrix the entry to the tail is worked out from the main task and the centre of the chart: M = D + centre. For the Devil (15) to stand at the entry when Temperance (14) is the task, the centre would have to equal one — the Magician. But the Magician never stands at the centre of a personal chart: the centre can only hold the numbers from 3 to 14, plus 16, 18, 20 and 22. So in one person the road from the Devil to Temperance never begins — there is no conjurer to turn one into the other.

In a couple the centre does not enter the tail: each point is the sum of the same points in two personal charts. The entry comes from two entries, the middle from two middles, the main task from two main tasks. That is how a triple appears which neither of the two has alone.

The second clue is the couple's centre. In 80.7% of couples with this tail it holds the Sun (19), in the remaining 19.3% the Wheel of Fortune (10). No date of birth puts the Sun at the centre of a personal matrix: this energy appears in the middle of the chart only when there are two people. The tail itself occurs in about one couple in 233 (0.429%) and ranks 63rd by frequency among the 97 couple tails.

So both this couple's path and its atmosphere are made of what neither partner has alone. That is why the story of this tail is not about the character of either partner but about the bond: what shapes it takes and how it changes.

sections.h2: The myth this couple lives in: Heracles and Omphale
paragraphs: The strongest man of Greek myth was once sold. In Apollodorus' Library (II.6.2–3), Heracles, “going mad again”, threw his guest Iphitus from the walls of Tiryns and fell gravely ill. The oracle at Delphi gave its answer: “for him to be sold, and to serve for three years, and to pay compensation for the murder”. “Hermes sold Hercules, and he was bought by Omphale”, queen of Lydia. Pherecydes, as reported by an ancient commentator on the Odyssey, gives the price: three talents. In Sophocles' Women of Trachis the term is shorter: “a whole year”, “a bought slave to the barbarian Omphale”.

From there the myth breaks into scenes that Roman poets retold with obvious relish. Omphale puts on the skin of the Nemean lion and takes up the club. Heracles, in her dress, sits among her maids spinning wool. And the story has two endings. In Diodorus of Sicily (IV.31) the queen learned who he was, marvelled at his valour, set him free, married him and bore him a son. In Sophocles, Heracles came back from Lydia sworn to enslave the man he blamed for his shame — and the chain moved on.

The three acts of the myth fall onto the three cards of the tail. The purchase is the Devil: a bond that begins with the word “mine”. The lion skin on someone else's shoulders is Strength: the dispute over who holds the power. The exchange of clothes and two couches side by side are Temperance: a measure in which each stays themselves. This is our reading, not a meaning taken from the books: neither Waite nor Lisovskaya writes about Heracles. But the matches are too close to pass by. Latin verse and Saint-Saëns' French are given in our own literal translation; Apollodorus, Diodorus and Sophocles are quoted in the translations by Frazer, Oldfather and Jebb.

sections.h2: Entry to the task, 15: the language of “you're mine”
paragraphs: The entry to a couple's tail is what the two want together, their agreements and their “common language”. In the compatibility reading the same point also appears in the sphere “Relationship and common language”, labelled “Common language”. For this couple, the common language is the Devil's.

The Romans turned it into a whole genre. Love elegy calls the beloved domina — the word a slave used for his mistress — and the lover her slave. Tibullus opens elegy II.4: “Here I see slavery and a mistress waiting for me: farewell now, freedom of my fathers. A bitter slavery is given me, chains hold me, and Love never loosens the bonds of the wretched.” Propertius (III.11) asks a friend: “Why do you wonder if a woman turns my life around and drags under her laws a man handed over to her for debt?” — and a few lines later he remembers Omphale. Propertius' word addictus is legal: it meant a debtor whom the court had handed over to his creditor.

Two thousand years later the same language sounds in every couple, and hardly anyone notices it: “my other half”, “you belong to me”, “I'm all yours”. At the start of a union with this tail such words feel like the highest degree of closeness. The pull is strong, the passion real. Lisovskaya describes the Devil in a couple at its best as well: two people accept each other's dark sides, forgive mistakes and talk openly about what they want.

But the entry stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. One partner is late at work, the other sends a third message in a row, and it no longer says “miss you” but “where are you”. A gift that makes it awkward to say no. Shared passwords “because we have nothing to hide”. The urge to hold on through intimacy, money, a shared child or status — Lisovskaya lists this among the Devil's tasks in a couple, next to keeping silent about one's own wishes. Her closing thought on the fifteenth energy is short: nobody belongs to anybody.

Diodorus has a detail that explains how this happens. Heracles, he writes, “willingly submitted to be sold”, and Omphale bought a slave without knowing who he was: who he was and whose son, she learned later. Only a stranger can be owned. Ownership begins where a role, an image, a function stands in place of a person, and “mine” often answers the question “whose are you?” that gets asked instead of “who are you?”.

Wen adds an important caveat to the Devil: the card “does not necessarily mean the Seeker is entirely to blame”. The Seeker “is not entirely innocent”, but “the greater culpability rests elsewhere”. The myth says the same. In Sophocles the herald asks that no offence be taken at his tale of the sale, since “the deed is found to be Zeus' work”. In this tail the Devil is not the vice of one partner but the shape of the bond the couple starts with. The numbers show this even more clearly, but more on them below.

sections.h2: Middle of the task, 11: who wears the lion skin
paragraphs: The Nemean lion was Heracles' first labour. Its skin, which no weapon could pierce, became his armour and his mark. And it is this skin that Omphale puts on in Lydia. In Ovid's Fasti (II.325) the queen “herself takes the heavy club and the lion's spoil”. In the Heroides, Heracles' wife Deianira writes him a letter full of bitter irony: “You are deceived and do not know it: these are not the lion's spoils but yours. You conquered the beast; she conquered you” (IX.113–114). And further: Omphale “armed her hand with the club, tamer of beasts, and saw in the mirror her consort's arms” (IX.117–118).

The middle of a couple's tail is how the two live the path from the entry to the main task. For this couple the path runs through Strength, that is, through the question “who wins?”. Lisovskaya describes Strength in a couple both ways. At its worst: a fight for leadership, each with their own truth, mockery and humiliation, one partner openly dominating. At its best: the two charge and strengthen each other, sense what the other needs, and one accepts the other's lead where the other is stronger.

The myth shows both. Almost nineteen centuries after Ovid, Camille Saint-Saëns wrote the symphonic poem Le Rouet d'Omphale (Omphale's Spinning Wheel, 1871–1872) and explained its subject himself: “la séduction féminine, la lutte triomphante de la faiblesse contre la force” — feminine seduction, the triumphant struggle of weakness against strength. The spinning wheel, he said, was only a pretext for the rhythm, and an attentive listener would hear “Hercules groaning in bonds he cannot break, and Omphale mocking the hero's vain efforts”. The bonds come from the Devil at the entry, the mockery from Strength at its worst: a victory celebrated over the defeated.

There is another side too. Propertius (III.11.17–20) writes that Omphale rose to such glory that the man who had set up his pillars in a world he had pacified “drew out soft wool with so hard a hand”. Deianira adds that Heracles' “too-mighty hands” more than once crushed the spindles as he twisted the thread with hard fingers (IX.79–80). Strength used to strangling lions cannot hold a spindle: it breaks what is fine. This is the turn towards the main task — strength needs measure.

The history of the card repeats the myth. On one of the oldest surviving tarot cards, from the Milanese Visconti-Sforza deck (about 1450–1480, now in the Morgan Library in New York), Strength is a man who “raises club in both hands above lion”; he is usually taken to be Heracles. Later the lion stays on the card, but beside it stands a woman, and she does not strike it. Over a few centuries the symbol of Strength walked Omphale's path itself: the lion passed from a hero with a club to a woman with bare hands.

Wen explains the difference. The Chariot is “strength to master the world”, Strength is “strength to master the self”. Under this card, she writes, “the Seeker cannot use brute force to exercise will over others; the Seeker must use gentle, subtle influence.” For a couple this means the middle is passed not when someone has won but when the skin can move from shoulders to shoulders and come back. Today one leads the renovation, tomorrow the other handles the bank, and nobody wears the skin as a trophy.

sections.h2: Main task, 14: two couches side by side
paragraphs: A couple's main task is the point that says what the two have to learn, and it is read mostly through what does not work. For Temperance, Lisovskaya says it plainly: one partner always gives way and the other does not even think of it. One saves, the other spends. There is no common language, and at times it is unclear why the relationship exists at all. The task is to reach agreement, not to load one's own fears and wishes onto the partner and not to try to control them.

The most exact scene for this task is in Ovid's Fasti (II.303–358). Ovid explains why the god Faunus dislikes clothes and tells “an old tale full of fun”. Omphale and Heracles are walking to the vineyards of Tmolus. Above the queen is a golden parasol against the warm sun, “and yet it was Hercules' hands that held it”. In a cave, while the servants prepare supper and wine, she dresses Alcides in her own things: fine tunics dyed with Gaetulian purple, her slender girdle. The girdle is too small. To free his huge hands he loosens the ties of the tunic, bracelets not made for such wrists snap, and his big feet tear the “little bonds” of her sandals. She herself takes the heavy club, the lion skin and the arrows.

Here the Latin keeps a clue. Ovid's word for ties and straps is vincula, the same word as Tibullus' “bonds”: “Love never loosens the bonds” (numquam vincla remittit). In the cave Heracles “loosens the ties of the tunics” himself (tunicarum vincla relaxat). One word. In the elegy nobody loosens the bonds; in the scene of exchange the one who wears them loosens them, and the little straps tear at the first step. A chain stops being a chain when the two take turns wearing it.

Then comes the detail that makes the whole scene worth reading. After supper they lie down to sleep “on couches set side by side, apart” (et positis iuxta secubuere toris): in the morning they are to hold a rite for Bacchus, “the discoverer of the vine”, and must come to it pure. Side by side and not merged. Close, and each on their own couch. This is Temperance in a couple: not one cup for two but two cups, with movement between them.

At midnight Faunus creeps into the cave. In the same book Ovid calls him two-horned and horn-hoofed (II.268, II.361); that look, the horns and goat legs, would later pass to the devil. “What does shameless love not dare?” Faunus gropes his way to the first couch, touches the coarse bristles of the lion skin and pulls his hand back in fear — as a traveller pulls back his foot on seeing a snake. On the next couch his fingers find soft cloth, and he is “deceived by a lying sign”. He climbs onto the couch — and Heracles throws him to the floor. The queen calls her servants and asks for light, everything lies open in the glow, and everyone laughs: the servants, Heracles himself, the Lydian queen. Ever since, Ovid concludes, the god who was fooled by a dress has disliked clothes that deceive the eyes, and calls his worshippers to his rites naked.

Our reading: the horned god goes by signs. Bristles mean danger, softness means prey. Swapping roles leaves him nothing to hold on to. And a second point: Heracles in a woman's tunic is still Heracles and throws the intruder off in one move. The exchange does not take strength away; it teaches when to use it.

Wen has a thought about Temperance, said about work but just as true of a couple: “it isn't that new skills need to be learned, but rather that the Seeker need only reconcile his or her existing skills with the task at hand.” A couple with this tail does not need to become different people. It needs to learn to pour. Today one carries the household, tomorrow the other. Money is not “in one pair of hands, by the rules” but in a shared decision. “I'll give way this time” does not turn into “I always give way”. A simple test is to recall who gave way over the last month. If the answer is always the same person, Temperance is at its worst even when there are no quarrels.

The Heroides have one more detail: Heracles “weighs back equal portions” of wool “to his beautiful mistress” (IX.78). A pensum was a spinner's day's work, wool weighed out on scales; in German, Pensum still means a workload. This couple's main task is the same day's work, only now both hold the scales.

sections.h2: What Waite drew: a ring before the altar, a lion and two cups
paragraphs: On Waite's cards the three points of the tail look like one bond in three states.

**The Devil.** “The Horned Goat of Mendes” stands on an altar, a distant relative of Ovid's Faunus. “There is a ring in front of the altar, from which two chains are carried to the necks of two figures, male and female.” Waite likens them to Adam and Eve after the Fall and writes: “Hereof is the chain and fatality of the material life.” “The figures are tailed, to signify the animal nature, but there is human intelligence in the faces.” An altar, a ring, a man and a woman: take away the horned figure and it is the layout of a wedding. Our reading: a union that begins with a ring becomes a chain when someone else holds the ring — habit, fear, “that's how it's done”.

**Strength.** A woman “is closing the jaws of a lion”; “her beneficent fortitude has already subdued the lion, which is being led by a chain of flowers”. “There is one aspect in which the lion signifies the passions,” Waite writes, “and she who is called Strength is the higher nature in its liberation.”

**Temperance.** A winged figure is “pouring the essences of life from chalice to chalice. It has one foot upon the earth and one upon waters.” When the rule of this card holds in our consciousness, according to Waite, “it tempers, combines and harmonises the psychic and material natures.”

Waite also gives a bridge to the couple's centre. Of the Sun he writes that the renewed mind “leads forth the animal nature in a state of perfect conformity”. The same animal nature that sits on a chain in the Devil walks alongside of its own accord in the Sun. The chain holds, the flowers lead, the water flows, the light reveals: the four cards of this couple are four shapes of one bond.

sections.h2: Two endings: the chain is passed on or taken off
paragraphs: The myth has two endings, and both are in the books.

**Sophocles.** The herald tells Heracles' wife that the year of slavery stung the hero so deeply that he swore “to enslave with wife and child the man who had brought that suffering upon him”. He kept the oath: the city of Eurytus was destroyed and its captive women were sent to Heracles' house. Then the tragedy of the Women of Trachis begins. Deianira, afraid of losing her husband, sends him a robe soaked in a centaur's blood: she had been told it would bring back his love. The robe clings to his body and burns like fire; Heracles dies of that torment. Clothing is again at the centre of the story, but now it is not an exchange but an attempt to hold on, and it destroys. The one who was bought starts buying: a chain that is not taken off gets passed on.

**Diodorus.** Omphale sees her slave's courage, learns who he is and who his parents were, “marvelled at his valour, set him free, and marrying him bore him Lamus”. The order is what matters: first know, then free, then choose. The marriage Diodorus puts at the end is possible only between free people.

For a couple with the 15-11-14 tail this is not a forecast of how things will end but two directions that every union with these numbers has. The couple can keep swapping slave and master: today one holds on, tomorrow the other gets even. Or it can cancel the purchase itself — stop asking “whose are you?” and start asking “who are you?”.

sections.h2: Clues in the numbers: a queen and a lion-tamer
paragraphs: A couple's tail is made of two personal tails, and 15-11-14 has only three such combinations: 6-17-11 + 9-12-3 (88% of couples), 12-16-4 + 3-13-10 (10%) and 6-14-8 + 9-15-6 (2%). Every number in them is a clue.

**Nobody brings the Devil.** In 98% of couples with this tail neither of the two personal tails contains a fifteen: the Devil appears only in the sum. Only in the rare combination 6-14-8 + 9-15-6 does it stand in the middle of one partner's personal tail. This couple's chain belongs to neither partner alone — the two forge it together, which is why looking for someone to blame in it is pointless.

**The entry: a hermit and lovers.** In 90% of couples the entry is the sum of 9 and 6: one partner's personal tail begins with the Hermit, the other's with the Lovers. Our reading: one comes into closeness from solitude, the other from the wish to merge. When these two wishes — to keep a distance and to be together — add up, a chain appears: one holds on for fear of losing, the other keeps a distance for fear of dissolving, and the harder the first pulls, the harder the second resists. In the remaining 10% the entry is the Hanged Man (12) and the Empress (3).

**A middle made of the ends.** In 88% of couples the middle is the Hanged Man and the Star (12 + 17), in 10% the Tower and Death (16 + 13). And in 2% it is Temperance and the Devil (14 + 15): in these couples the middle of the tail is literally built from its two ends, and Strength is born where the Devil meets Temperance.

**The main task: a queen and a lion-tamer.** In 88% of couples Temperance is 3 + 11: one partner's personal tail ends with the Empress, the other's with Strength. The myth puts a queen beside the man who killed the lion; the numbers put the same two cards side by side. We do not present this as a law: the meaning of a personal tail does not carry over to a couple's tail; the point is only what the number is made of. In 10% of couples the task is the sum of the Emperor and the Wheel of Fortune (4 + 10), in 2% of Justice and the Lovers (8 + 6).

sections.h2: The Sun at the centre: what daylight shows
paragraphs: A couple's centre is the atmosphere inside the union, what happens between the two when nobody is watching. In 80.7% of couples with this tail it holds the Sun, in 19.3% the Wheel of Fortune.

In Waite's list of divinatory meanings the Sun has three entries: “Material happiness, fortunate marriage, contentment.” At its best, Lisovskaya names for the Sun at a couple's centre respect, harmony, each partner's success in their own field, and the sense of one partner being under the other's protection. The Fasti has a picture for this: Heracles holding a golden parasol against the sun over Omphale. At its worst the same centre brings tyranny and total control, limits on the partner's self-realisation, comparisons. The Sun lights up what is already in the couple, and if the entry says “you're mine”, the light only makes it more visible.

One more observation from Ovid: the trick with the clothes works only in the dark. As soon as the lights were brought, “everything lay open”, and everyone laughed, Heracles included. This tail's Devil lives at night, in what is left unsaid. The Sun at the centre is laughter in daylight, when the swap of roles is visible to both and becomes a game rather than a trap.

The Wheel of Fortune at the centre (19.3%) is an atmosphere in which roles go round: the skin is on one partner today and on the other tomorrow. At its best Lisovskaya describes such an atmosphere as the feeling of a fated meeting and the ability to accept the partner in any state; at its worst, the two do not hear each other and blame fate.

sections.h2: The couple's values: the Empress, the World, the Hanged Man
paragraphs: The sphere “The couple's values” answers what the union exists for. In couples with the 15-11-14 tail it most often holds the Empress (52.9%), then the World (25.7%) and the Hanged Man (21.3%).

The Empress is a home, a full table, what grows and bears fruit; in Waite her list begins “Fruitfulness, action, initiative”. In the myth she is a queen in her own kingdom, and the value here is not power over the other but a shared household that feeds both. The World is a wholeness in which each has a place. The Hanged Man is the value of a pause and of a different angle: to stop and look at the familiar upside down. For a couple learning to swap roles this makes particular sense. The last two readings are ours.
The personal matrix for 19.03.1979 gives the tail 9-12-3 and the centre 6; the matrix for 05.11.1975 gives the tail 6-17-11 and the centre 13. The couple's points add up pair by pair:

In this tail the middle happens to equal the sum of its ends (15 + 14 = 29 → 11), but it is not worked out that way; it comes from the two personal middles, and here the match is a coincidence, not a rule. “The couple's values” here is the Empress (3).

For this couple the numbers of the tail also recur in other spheres. Temperance also stands in the sphere “Why you met”, at the point “What to create together” (3 + 11 = 14): what the couple has to learn and what it is here to create are one and the same. Strength also stands in the sphere “What fills the union” (22 + 16 = 38 → 11): the trial of strength does not only test these two, it also charges them. Not every couple with this tail has this — it belongs to these particular dates.
There are no other couple tails made of 15, 11 and 14: in the method this triple occurs only in this order.

sections.h2: How to live this tail at its best

ul: **Ask “who are you?”, not “whose are you?”.** Take an interest in what the partner wants, not only in where they have been. Diodorus puts this first: first know, then free.
**Agree who wears the skin where.** Money, renovation, relatives, holidays — each area has its own lead, and every few months this is reviewed out loud.

**Swap roles for real.** Whoever usually drives rides as a passenger for a week; whoever plans everything hands the planning over. Not as a punishment, but as in Omphale's cave: with supper and laughter.
**Laugh together, not at each other.** Laughter in daylight is this couple's Sun; mockery of the defeated is Strength at its worst.
**Leave each other a couch of your own.** Close people need the right to be side by side and apart: their own time, their own affairs, their own silence.
**Count who gives way.** If over a month it was always the same person, that is not peace but Temperance at its worst.
**Do not hold on.** Not with a gift, money, intimacy or a child. In Sophocles, the robe sent to bind ends up burning.

paragraphs: If “you're mine” turns into surveillance, threats or fear, it is no longer the story of the tail and not a task for patience. Then it is time for help from a psychologist, and in danger — a call to the local emergency number.

ul: **Entry to the task — 15, the Devil.** What the couple wants together and the language it speaks: “mine”, “all mine”, “I can't live without you”. The pull is real, and the same pull turns into resistance when the wish to be together becomes the wish to hold on.

**Middle of the task — 11, Strength.** How the couple moves on: through a trial of strength. Who decides, who gives way, who holds the power. At its best, strength passes from hand to hand and comes back; at its worst, it has to be proved.
**Main task — 14, Temperance.** Learning measure and exchange: the same person should not always give way, each should know the weight of the other's load, and neither should dissolve into the other.

intro: An ancient myth tells this path almost word for word. Heracles was sold as a slave to Omphale, queen of Lydia; she put on his lion skin, he sat down to her wool, and in one version it all ended in freedom and a wedding, in another in a new chain. What follows is an investigation: what the cards themselves say, what Waite, Wen and Lisovskaya write, and what the numbers show when every date is checked.

faq.q: What does karmic tail 15-11-14 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the couple's task to travel from “you're mine” to “us”. The entry is the Devil: a strong pull and a wish to belong to each other that easily becomes a wish to own. The middle is Strength: a trial of strength and the question of who holds the power. The main task is Temperance: learning exchange and measure so that the same person does not always give way.

faq.q: Is this a bad tail for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail describes a task, not a verdict, and it is read mostly through what there is to learn. The Devil at the entry gives this couple a rare power of attraction, Strength in the middle gives energy, and in 80.7% of such couples the Sun stands at the centre, which for Waite means, among other things, “fortunate marriage”. The difficulty is one: not to confuse closeness with ownership.

faq.q: Can 15-11-14 be a personal karmic tail?
faq.a: No. In a personal chart the entry to the tail equals the main task plus the centre, and with Temperance as the task, the Devil at the entry would need a centre of 1, the Magician. The Magician never appears at the centre of a personal matrix, so only two people can make this triple.

faq.q: Who is Heracles and who is Omphale in the couple?
faq.a: Both, in turn. The partners' sex does not assign the roles: either can wear the skin, and the whole meaning of the middle of the tail is that it moves from shoulders to shoulders. Getting stuck in one role — “I always decide” or “I always give way” — is exactly what this couple is learning to leave behind.

faq.q: How is the couple tail 15-11-14 calculated?
faq.a: Work out each partner's personal destiny matrix and add the matching points of their tails: entry to entry, middle to middle, main task to main task, reducing any sum above 22 by adding its digits. For example, 19.03.1979 and 05.11.1975 give 9 + 6 = 15, 12 + 17 = 29 → 11 and 3 + 11 = 14.

report: The main task is Temperance, and it is read through what does not work: one partner always gives way and the other does not even think of it; one saves, the other spends. The most exact scene for this task is in Ovid's Fasti. In a cave Omphale dresses Heracles in her tunics and girdle. The girdle is too small; to free his hands he loosens the ties, the bracelets snap, his feet tear the sandal straps.

The Latin keeps a clue. Ovid's word for the ties is vincula, the same word as Tibullus' “bonds”. In the elegy Love never loosens the bonds; in the cave Heracles loosens them himself. **A chain stops being a chain when the two take turns wearing it.**

Then they lie down to sleep “on couches set side by side, apart”: a rite awaits in the morning, and they must come to it pure. Side by side and not merged — not one cup for two but two cups, with movement between them. At midnight goat-legged Faunus creeps into the cave. He gropes the lion skin and pulls his hand back in fear, finds soft cloth, climbs onto the couch — and Heracles throws him to the floor. Lights are brought, and everyone laughs. The horned god goes by signs, and swapping roles leaves him nothing to hold on to. And Heracles in a woman's tunic is still Heracles: the exchange does not take strength away, it teaches when to use it.

report.h3: The chain is passed on or taken off

report: The myth has two endings. In Sophocles, Heracles comes back sworn to enslave the man he blames, and tragedy follows: his wife, afraid of losing him, sends him a robe meant to bring back his love, and the robe burns him like fire. The one who was bought starts buying. In Diodorus, Omphale learns who stands before her, marvels at him, sets him free — and only then marries him. **First know, then free, then choose.**
This is not a forecast but two directions open to a couple with this tail. What helps to choose the second:

ul: asking what the partner wants, not only where they have been;
agreeing who leads in which area, and reviewing it out loud from time to time;
swapping roles for real, not as a punishment, with supper and laughter;
laughing together, not at each other;
leaving each other the right to be side by side and apart;
noticing who gave way over the last month: if it was always the same person, that is not peace but Temperance at its worst;
not holding on with a gift, money or intimacy.

report: If “you're mine” turns into surveillance, threats or fear, it is no longer the story of the tail and not a task for patience. Then it is time for help from a psychologist, and in danger — a call to a local emergency number or crisis line.

unit.title: A lion skin for two

captions.M: Wanting to belong to each other completely
captions.N: Finding out who wins, and handing over the lead
captions.D: Swapping roles so it is not always one who yields

unit.meaning: Your task is to get from “you're mine” to “us”: to know each other rather than own each other, and to take turns giving way.
